extracted.intended_audience: science press officers, science communicators, journalists, and researchers studying science communication
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating health-related science press releases for exaggeration and fidelity to the source paper, focusing on advice strength, causal language, presentation of non-human research, and inclusion of caveats/limitations. Intended to guide production and assessment of press releases so news coverage does not amplify misleading claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health Advice Level (four-level scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers coded advice across four levels: None; Implicit (e.g., 'these findings suggest that mid-late childhood may be the best'); Explicit (non-reader directed); Explicit (to reader/public). Press releases containing stronger advice than journal articles were classified as exaggerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score the press release's advice on this four-point scale and compare to the source paper; if the press release gives stronger, more prescriptive advice than the paper, mark as an exaggeration. Examples: implicit wording ('these findings suggest...') vs explicit reader-directed recommendations ('You should...'). Note caveats are rare in advice statements (present in ~15%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal Claims (seven-point determinism scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in titles and opening sentences were coded with seven strength levels: No statement; Explicit statement of no relation; Correlational language ('associated with'); Ambiguous phrasing ('linked to'); Conditional causation ('might increase'); Potential causation ('can increase'); Unconditional causation ('increases'). The focus was on studies using correlational designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating press releases, code causal language in titles and ledes using this seven-point scale and compare it to the paper's claims and study design. For correlational studies, stronger causal language (e.g., 'increases') in a press release than in the paper indicates exaggeration. Prefer correlational phrasing ('associated with') when appropriate. Use the scale to detect gradations from no relation to unconditional causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human Inference Framing for Non-Human Research
rubrics_metrics.description: For animal, cellular, or simulation studies, statements were categorized as: Explicitly non-human; Implicitly human; Explicitly human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure press releases do not present non-human research as if findings directly apply to humans. Code and flag instances where non-human work is described implicitly or explicitly as human-relevant. Explicitly state the model (e.g., 'in mice', 'in cell cultures') and avoid wording that implies direct human outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match advice level to source paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should match the strength and direction of health or behavioral advice to that given in the source peer-reviewed paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the press release's advice statements to the source article; avoid increasing the prescriptiveness or scope of recommendations. If the paper offers none or only cautious/implicit suggestions, the press release should not present explicit public-directed advice. This is a primary indicator of exaggeration in press releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match causal language strength to source paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal language used in press releases should reflect the evidence and claims in the original paper (e.g., avoid causal wording for correlational studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align wording with study design: for correlational studies use correlational/associative terms; reserve causal verbs ('increases', 'causes') for appropriately designed causal studies. Assess titles and opening sentences carefully, since these were the coding targets in the study and strongly influence downstream news phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make non-human research scope explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: When research is based on animals, cells, or simulations, press releases should explicitly state that the findings are non-human and avoid implying direct human applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label the study population/model clearly (e.g., 'in mice', 'in vitro'); avoid vague terms ('linked to') that may invite human inference. The study found lower rates of non-human exaggeration from university press offices than other sources, suggesting explicit statements reduce misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include caveats and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should include caveats and limitations of the research. In the study, caveats were present in only ~15% of advice statements and ~14% of causal claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear caveats/limitations in press releases; the paper found that caveats in press releases strongly predicted their appearance in news stories (odds ratios ~9.5–9.6) and, importantly, did not reduce journalistic interest or coverage. Use caveats to reduce exaggeration without fearing decreased news uptake.
